html:
The Blood Telegram was a cable sent on 6 April 1971 from the American consulate in Dhaka to Washington, protesting the United States' silence over the army's killing in East Pakistan.

It was drafted by Consul General Archer Blood and signed by about twenty consulate staff. Titled "Selective Genocide", it said the government had failed to denounce the atrocities after Operation Searchlight, and that this was a moral failure. It was one of the strongest dissents ever sent by American diplomats.

President Richard Nixon and Henry Kissinger did not act on it. They valued General Yahya Khan as the private channel for the opening to China, and saw India as close to the Soviets. Blood was recalled in June and given a desk job. The foreign service later gave him an award for constructive dissent.

The cable gave the name to Gary Bass's 2013 book The Blood Telegram, and it remains central to the debate on American policy in the Bangladesh genocide.
sum: The Blood Telegram was a cable sent on 6 April 1971 from the American consulate in Dhaka to Washington, protesting the United States' silence over the army's killing in East Pakistan.
